prompt: What is a Playwright worker?

choices.text: A tab the runner opens inside one shared browser
choices.why: Each worker has a browser of its own; tabs in one browser would share far more than workers do.

choices.text: A separate Node process that runs whole files in a browser of its own
choices.why: Right. The runner hands each worker whole files, and the worker launches its own browser for them.

choices.text: A thread inside the runner that shares its memory
choices.why: Workers are processes, not threads; they share nothing in memory with the runner or each other.

choices.text: A separate machine in CI that runs one shard
choices.why: That is a shard's job. Workers all run on one machine.

prompt: A laptop has 12 logical processors. `playwright.config.js` sets no `workers` and the command line has no `--workers`. How many workers does `npx playwright test` start, at most?
hint: The default is a percentage of `os.cpus().length`, rounded down.

prompt: Three test files, twelve tests between them, are run with `--workers 4`. The summary says *using 3 workers*. Why not four?

choices.text: Playwright keeps one worker free for the shop
choices.why: The shop is started by `webServer` in the runner's own process tree; no worker is set aside for it.

choices.text: Four is more than half of the four processors, so it is cut
choices.why: Half the processors is only the default; `--workers 4` overrides it and is obeyed.

choices.text: The unit handed out is a file, and there were three files
choices.why: Right. Without `fullyParallel` a file's tests stay together in one worker; `--fully-parallel` used all four.

choices.text: One worker crashed while starting and was not replaced
choices.why: Every test passed and nothing crashed; the count was decided before any worker started.

prompt: A file creates a customer in its first test and checks the customer's page in its second. Somebody adds `fullyParallel: true` to the whole configuration. What is the likely result?

choices.text: Nothing changes, because tests in one file always share a worker
choices.why: That is the default, and `fullyParallel` is exactly the setting that ends it.

choices.text: Playwright notices the dependency and keeps the two tests in order
choices.why: Playwright cannot see what one test leaves for another; only the file's own configuration can say it.

choices.text: The run refuses to start until the file is marked serial
choices.why: Nothing checks this; the run starts and the failure arrives later.

choices.text: Each test becomes its own unit, and the written order is lost
choices.why: Right. Each test becomes its own unit of work, so the order the file was written in no longer holds; `mode: 'serial'` keeps that file together.

prompt: Two four-worker runs of the same suite, a minute apart, fail on different tests. What does that say about the cause?

choices.text: The cause moved, so there are two defects to find
choices.why: The cause, one shared shop, was the same both times; only which tests overlapped changed.

choices.text: The failing tests are flaky on their own and need retries
choices.why: Alone, with one worker, every one of them passed; they fail because of what other tests did.

choices.text: The machine was too slow for four workers
choices.why: The errors are wrong counts, `Received: "2"`, not timeouts on a slow page.

choices.text: Which tests lose depends on which ones share a second
choices.why: Right. The victims follow the timing of each run; the shared basket stays put.

prompt: Every basket test starts with `request.post('/api/reset')` in a `beforeEach`. Why does that not protect it under four workers?

choices.text: The reset is asynchronous and is not awaited
choices.why: It is awaited; the basket really is empty when the test goes on.

choices.text: It empties the shop at one moment, and the test goes on assuming it
choices.why: Right. The test assumes the shop stays empty until its assertion, and nothing makes it so.

choices.text: Each worker has its own copy of the shop, so the reset reaches the wrong one
choices.why: There is one shop, started once by `webServer`; that is the whole problem.

choices.text: Resets are skipped when tests run in parallel
choices.why: They run every time, and each one can also empty somebody else's basket halfway through.

prompt: A test about the offer and a test that signs up a new customer never touch the basket. Why can they still break each other, or a basket test, in this shop?

choices.text: `reset()` empties all three at once
choices.why: Right. Any test that resets wipes all three, which is how `cache.spec.js:7` read the old mango offer after posting a new one.

choices.text: Both run on the same port, and a port serves one test at a time
choices.why: A server on one port answers many requests at once; the shared state is the problem, not the port.

choices.text: Browser contexts share cookies between workers
choices.why: Lesson 10 showed contexts share no cookies; the shop sets none anyway.

choices.text: They cannot; only basket tests collide
choices.why: The four-worker runs failed an offer test too, `cache.spec.js:7`.

prompt: `turns.config.js` lists the files that leave the shop alone, not the files that touch it. What does that choice buy when somebody adds a new test file next month?

choices.text: The new file runs in parallel, so the suite stays fast
choices.why: That is what the other list would do, and it is how an unclassified file that resets the basket turns runs red.

choices.text: Playwright refuses to run a file that is on neither list
choices.why: `testIgnore` sends every unlisted file to the second project; nothing is refused.

choices.text: It waits its turn until somebody checks it
choices.why: Right. A list of safe files fails closed: forgetting to classify costs time, not a wrong result.

choices.text: Nothing: the two lists are equivalent
choices.why: They agree on today's files and disagree on every file written later.

prompt: In the second `turns.config.js`, the line that puts the one-at-a-time project in a phase of its own, after the other project, reads `___: ['parallel'],`.
hint: It is the property that names a project which must finish first.

prompt: With `workers: 1` on the one-at-a-time project and no `dependencies`, an eight-worker run started three of its files at once. What does Playwright 1.56's dispatcher count before handing out such a file?

choices.text: The files of that project already finished
choices.why: Finished files do not matter to a ceiling on what runs at once.

choices.text: Busy processes already running its files
choices.why: Right. A worker being swapped over from `parallel` is busy but still counted as `parallel`, so several can be handed one-at-a-time files together.

choices.text: The processors that are idle at that moment
choices.why: The dispatcher never looks at processors; the worker count was decided at the start.

choices.text: The tests in the file, and it refuses files with more than one
choices.why: A project's `workers` limits workers, not tests per file.

prompt: Why does adding more workers not bring the `turns.config.js` run below the time of its one-at-a-time phase?

choices.text: That phase runs its tests one after another in a single worker
choices.why: Right. Its total is a floor; extra workers can only speed up the `parallel` phase.

choices.text: Playwright ignores `--workers` when a configuration has projects
choices.why: The summary still said *using 4 workers* and *using 8 workers*; the total is obeyed.

choices.text: The shop answers only one request at a time
choices.why: The shop answered four workers at once in every red run; that was the trouble.

choices.text: The dependency makes every test wait for the slowest test of the suite
choices.why: It makes one project wait for the other, once; it does not tie each test to the slowest one.

prompt: How does Playwright decide which tests go into `--shard=2/3`?

choices.text: By the durations of the last run, so each shard takes the same time
choices.why: It keeps no durations between runs; the three shards here took different times.

choices.text: At random, with a seed taken from the shard number
choices.why: The cut is deterministic: the same suite lists the same tests for a shard every time.

choices.text: By counting tests, dealing out whole groups in order
choices.why: Right. `filterForShard` divides the test count by the shards and never splits a group, which is a whole file unless it is fully parallel.

choices.text: By file name, alphabetically, a third of the files each
choices.why: Files are not what is counted; a file matters only as a group that is never split.

prompt: One shard of a three-shard CI run is always the slowest, and its list shows one file whose tests each wait several seconds. What helps without new machines?

choices.text: Splitting it, or marking it fully parallel
choices.why: Right. A file is dealt out whole, so it pulls its shard along; smaller groups spread the wait.

choices.text: Running that shard with `--retries 2`
choices.why: Retries rerun failures; they make a slow shard slower, never faster.

choices.text: Renaming the file so it sorts into another shard
choices.why: It moves the slow file to another shard, which then becomes the slow one.

choices.text: Using `merge-reports`, which balances the shards when it merges them
choices.why: It only reads finished zip files into one report; the shards have already run.

prompt: Put a three-shard CI run in order, from the jobs starting to the single report.
items: Three jobs each run `npx playwright test --shard=N/3` with the blob reporter
Each job saves the zip its blob reporter wrote
A last job collects the three zips into one folder
`npx playwright merge-reports` turns the folder into one report
trap: The merge cannot start before the slowest shard has written its zip.

prompt: Sharded three ways with `turns.config.js`, where `one-at-a-time` depends on `parallel`, the merged report counted 121 tests for a suite of 61. Why?

choices.text: The blob reporter wrote every result twice
choices.why: Each zip held what its shard ran; the shards really ran 42, 40 and 39 tests.

choices.text: Each shard reran the dependency
choices.why: Right. After the shard filter, Playwright adds back every project a picked one depends on, whole: 30 tests on each machine.

choices.text: `merge-reports` counts the retries of failed tests
choices.why: Nothing failed and nothing was retried; every shard was green.

choices.text: Three shards of 61 tests always add up to more than 61
choices.why: Split as two commands with `--no-deps`, the same three machines ran exactly 61.

prompt: A Selenium suite runs eight tests at once against a standalone grid that offered four Chrome slots. What happens to the other four?

choices.text: They fail with an error saying there is no free slot
choices.why: The grid does not refuse them; that is what its queue is for.

choices.text: The node opens four more slots, one per test
choices.why: The slots are fixed when the node starts; `--max-sessions` changes them, not demand.

choices.text: They wait in the session queue until a slot is released
choices.why: Right. The run then takes about as long as it would with four at once.

choices.text: They share the four browsers, two tests per browser
choices.why: A session is one browser for one test; nothing shares one.

prompt: Match each setting to what it limits.

pairs.right: how many Playwright workers run at once
how many test files `node --test` runs at once
how many browser sessions a grid node accepts at once
which slice of a Playwright suite this machine runs

prompt: In the curve, going from four workers to eight on the four-processor laptop made the run slower. What grew the most along the way?

choices.text: The number of tests, because each worker runs the suite again
choices.why: Every run had the same tests; workers share them out, they do not repeat them.

choices.text: The memory held and the processor time spent on the same work
choices.why: Right. Each worker adds a browser's memory, and past four the processors are shared out and switched between.

choices.text: The time each test waits for the shop to answer
choices.why: Waiting is what extra workers fill; the cost that grew was memory and processor time.

choices.text: Nothing measurable: the difference was noise
choices.why: Memory more than quadrupled from one worker to eight; that is not noise.

prompt: `measure.sh` adds up every process's resident memory. Why is its peak an overstatement of what the machine lost?

choices.text: It counts the memory of processes that had already exited
choices.why: A process that exited is not in `ps`; only the living tree is added.

choices.text: It measures in kilobytes and rounds up to megabytes
choices.why: Shell arithmetic divides and rounds down; the rounding is tiny either way.

choices.text: Shared pages are counted once per process
choices.why: Right. A shared page is resident in several processes and is added once per process; the figure is for comparing runs.

choices.text: It also counts the memory `ps` and `awk` use while sampling
choices.why: Those run under the script, not under the measured command, so they are outside the tree.

prompt: A CI machine has 2 processors. A teammate sets `workers: 8` there to make the suite faster, after it ran well with eight workers on a 16-thread laptop. What does this lesson predict?

choices.text: The same speed-up as on the laptop, since the suite is the same
choices.why: The gain came from processors the CI machine does not have.

choices.text: No change, because Playwright caps workers at the processor count
choices.why: Only the default is a share of the processors; an explicit number is obeyed.

choices.text: A slower run that holds more memory, and possibly timeouts
choices.why: Right. Eight browsers on two processors wait for turns while holding memory; measure on that machine and pick the count where time stops falling.

choices.text: A refusal to start, because eight is more than the processors
choices.why: Nothing checks it; eight workers start and compete.

prompt: The shop finally gets a basket per visitor, kept by a cookie. What should happen to `turns.config.js`?

choices.text: Keep it, because sharing a shop is always risky
choices.why: The risk was one basket for everybody; with a basket per context the basket tests no longer collide.

choices.text: Move every file into `leavesTheShopAlone` without looking
choices.why: The offer and the customers are still shared, and a reset still empties them for everyone.

choices.text: Delete the one-at-a-time project, as its comment says, once nothing shared is left
choices.why: Right. The comment names the reason for the cost, so the cost goes when the reason does; the offer and the reset are still to check first.

choices.text: Raise its `workers` from 1 to 4
choices.why: That keeps the project and its phase; the point was to stop needing them.
